first.rationale: I currently intend to test onboarding simplification because onboarding completion and activation are both declining, and prior evidence indicates shortening onboarding improves time-to-value and adoption. I want to verify the onboarding result and the promotional-pricing result before committing, since aggressive pricing may address competitive SMB losses but could create downstream qualified-revenue or customer-quality risk.

mid.rationale: Run a controlled onboarding-simplification experiment, prioritizing self-serve accounts where completion and activation are both declining. The verified result shows shortened onboarding increased completion, reduced time-to-value, and improved 30-day retention, while signup simplification also previously lifted SMB activation. Do not pursue promotional pricing: its qualified-revenue lift was offset by a 12% retention decline and poor first-renewal survival. Track activation, completion, time-to-value, 30-day retention, and qualified revenue with guardrails against downstream cohort-quality deterioration.

final2.rationale: Stay with the committed onboarding-simplification experiment rather than reactively switching to deep discounting. The verified onboarding result improved completion, time-to-value, and 30-day retention, directly addressing current activation and onboarding declines. Promotional pricing may blunt near-term SMB churn, but the verified cohort had a 12% retention decline and failed to survive the first renewal cycle, making it unsuitable for the sustainable qualified-revenue objective. Treat the competitor response as a risk signal to monitor, not a reason to override the current experiment without evidence that retention and renewal quality can be protected.
